summaries.summary: NMT depends on large-scale parallel data, performs poorly for low-resource or zero-resource pairs, and pivot-based translation doubles decoding time and propagates errors.
Transfer learning initializes a low-resource source→target child model from a high-resource pivot→target parent model but performs very poorly without child training data.
The language space mismatch problem, also named domain shift problem, causes zero-shot transfer failure because source and pivot feature distributions are not explicitly aligned.
The paper studies zero-shot transfer with source↔pivot and pivot↔target data, investigates two cross-lingual pre-training methods, and proposes BRidge Language Modeling (BRLM).
The paper proposes a new transfer learning approach for NMT using cross-lingual language model pre-training to enable high performance on zero-shot translation.
The paper proposes BRLM, a novel pre-training method that effectively alleviates the distance between different source language spaces.
The proposed approach significantly improves zero-shot translation, consistently surpassing pivoting and multilingual approaches while maintaining or improving supervised translation performance.
Existing zero-shot translation methods in NMT are mainly divided into pivot-based method, transfer learning, multilingual NMT, and unsupervised NMT.
Pivot-based Method includes pivoting and pivot-synthetic, but faces quadratic growth in source languages, high computation and parameter costs, and error propagation.
Transfer Learning for NMT uses a high-resource parent model and vocabulary or embedding improvements, but has limited effects in zero-shot translation.
Multilingual NMT supports multiple translation directions and unseen pairs but easily fails for zero-shot translation, is hyper-parameter sensitive, and often trails pivot-based methods.
Unsupervised NMT uses only large-scale monolingual corpora and performs well between similar languages but remains far from expectation between distant languages.
The proposed transfer learning method uses cross-lingual pre-training before parent model training so all source languages share the same feature space.
The approach is designed for zero-shot scenarios with source↔pivot and pivot↔target bilingual data but no source↔target parallel data.
The first step pre-trains a universal encoder with source/pivot monolingual or source↔pivot bilingual data.
The second step trains a pivot→target parent model on the pre-trained universal encoder while freezing several layers to avoid degeneracy.
The third step directly translates source sentences into target sentences with the parent model using the universal encoder.
The key difficulty is ensuring language-invariant intermediate representations, and the section presents two existing methods, a new method, and the transfer protocol.
Masked Language Modeling (MLM) and Translation Language Modeling (TLM) are effective on XNLI but understudied for cross-lingual generation in zero-shot conditions.
MLM uses BERT's Cloze objective on monolingual corpora, predicts [MASK]-replaced words, and maps shared word pieces into a shared space.
TLM extends MLM by concatenating sentence pairs, masking words in both sentences, and encouraging alignment of source and target representations.
BRidge Language Modeling (BRLM) is proposed to obtain word-level representation alignment by inferring masked words from aligned words on the other side.
BRLM stacks a shared encoder over both side sentences and includes Hard Alignment (BRLM-HA) and Soft Alignment (BRLM-SA) structures.
BRLM-HA uses an external aligner on source↔pivot data, masks source words, and predicts them using surrounding words and aligned pivot encoder outputs.
BRLM-SA uses an additional multi-head attention layer to learn alignment, avoid wrong external alignments, and enable many-to-one soft alignment.
MLM and TLM learn limited implicit alignment, while BRLM uses alignment information for better word-level representation alignment and reduced domain shift.
The transfer protocol considers a high resource pivot language with parallel data to source and target languages, divided into pretraining and transfer phases.
The pretraining phase pretrains MLM on source and pivot monolingual corpora, then TLM or BRLM on source-pivot parallel data to build a shared encoder.
The transfer phase trains a pivot→target NMT model initialized by the cross-lingually pre-trained encoder, freezes several layers, and transfers to source→target.
For scenarios with multiple source-side or target-side languages, the encoder and decoder are shared across each side languages for efficient deployment.
The approach is evaluated against strong baselines on Europarl and MultiUN, using BLEU as the automatic metric for translation evaluation.
Europarl evaluates Fr-En-Es, De-En-Fr and Ro-En-De with English as pivot, using devtest2006, test2006, 1,000 test sentences, 2,000 validation sentences, and 60K BPE tokens.
MultiUN uses English as pivot with Arabic, Spanish and Russian, yielding six zero-shot directions, 80K BPE splits, tokenize.perl tokenization, and lowercased data.
Baselines are traditional transfer learning, pivot-based method and multilingual NMT, with Transformer-big, 1024 units, 4096 feed-forward size, 6 layers, 8 heads, batch size 2400, and BLEU settings.
MLM+TLM and MLM+BRLM initialize from MLM, mask 15% of BPE tokens with 80% [MASK], 10% random and 10% unchanged, and use fastalign for BRLM-HA.
The approaches consistently outperform pivoting, MNMT and cross-lingual transfer without pretraining across languages and datasets, using one encoder-decoder model more efficiently than pivoting.
On Europarl, pivoting is the strongest baseline, while cross-lingual transfer without shared vocabularies performs worst for not using source↔pivot parallel data.
MLM+BRLM-SA improves by 0.9-4.8 BLEU points over pivoting on Europarl zero-shot directions and also improves supervised pivot→target translation.
MLM alone outperforms cross-lingual transfer and rivals pivoting, while MLM+BRLM-SA performs best and shows soft alignment is more helpful than hard alignment.
On MultiUN, MLM+BRLM-SA performs best among the proposed approaches and significantly outperforms MNMT among one encoder-decoder systems.
MLM+BRLM-SA with back translation outperforms pivoting_m by 2.4 BLEU points averagely and MNMT BIBREF22 by 4.6 BLEU points averagely.
Sentence representation analysis shows MLM+BRLM-SA has the most stable cross-lingual representations, while cosine similarity decreases as the number of layers increases.
Visualization of an English-Russian sentence pair shows MLM+BRLM-SA gives higher similarity for aligned words and better word-level representation alignment.
On MultiUN, updating all parameters causes catastrophic forgetting, freezing all parameters hurts supervised direction, and freezing the first four layers performs best.
The paper proposes cross-lingual pretraining based transfer for zero-shot translation, using one monolingual and two bilingual pretraining methods to build a universal encoder.
